blocks.text: The Hebrews in Kimchi anxiously ask where the ravens brought the bread and meat from. Some hold that they were taken from the table of Ahab, others from that of Jehoshaphat. As if the prophet, brought up in the utmost frugality, had needed royal fare. I would rather say that these things were set aside for the prophet by some one of those seven thousand who ^{b)} had not bowed the knee before Baal, whom God [col. 216] willed to be privy to so great a secret. Yet it is safest to answer with the author of the Mirabilia Scripturae, book 2, chapter 15: But whence that raven brought that meat and bread, let him see to it who entrusted it with such a task. Elsewhere ^{c)} an angel of God sets bread and water before this same Elias when he was hungry in the desert, which you will say was more fitting, and Θεοπρεπέστερον [theoprepesteron]. But God also willed the same [II, 809] service to be performed by ravens, to teach that all creatures are subject to his command ^{(4)}. But the raven, you will say, is an unclean bird, defiling everything by its touch. Quite so, since it mostly feeds on carcasses, and the ceremonial law counts it among the unclean birds. But what God has cleansed must not be held unclean, Act. X, 15. The same God who had enacted this law also abrogated it, or at least dispensed Elias from observing it for a time. Although there was no need of such a dispensation. For the observance of ceremonies could be set aside when the necessity of life pressed. Thus Samson was permitted to eat the honeycomb which bees had built in the dead lion, as Theodoret observes on this passage. And David, when hungry, ate without scruple the bread τῆς προθέσεως [tēs protheseōs], which otherwise it was not lawful to eat except for the priests alone, Luc. VI, 4. And accordingly it was rightly decreed that the Jews, when attacked by the enemy on the sabbath day, might fight and repel force with force, 1 Macchab. II, 41. For life was at stake. And the Sabbath is for man, not man for the Sabbath. Marc. II, 27. The author of the Mirabilia asserts that the ravens serving Elias made amends for the fault committed in the flood. The ravens, he says, are commanded to minister to the prophet, so that that bird might be seen to expiate the fault it had committed in the flood, by becoming a faithful servant to Elias, it which had before been negligent and deceitful toward Noah. Chrysostom, in the Sermon On Elias, holds that the Prophet was like the ravens in this: that as the raven is a μισότεκνον [misoteknon] animal, so Elias hated his children, namely the Jews, for their sins, and, having shut heaven by his prayers, had imposed a long famine on them. And that God therefore wished to soften the prophet's mind, exasperated beyond measure, by the example of the ravens, which, harsh and μισότεκνοι [misoteknoi] though they are, yet with a changed disposition now took pity on the prophet and supplied him with food lest he perish of hunger: as if he had said to Elias, Μὴ τοσαύτη παρὰ σοὶ μετὰ Ἰουδαίων μισοτεκνία, ὅση τοῖς κόραξι κατὰ τῶν νεοσσῶν τῶν οἰκείων. ἀλλ᾽ ὅρα νῦν μεταβεβλημένους τοὺς κόρακας. ὅρα τὴν ἐκείνων, ὦ Ἠλία, φιλανθρωπίαν. οἱ περὶ τοὺς οἰκείους ἀπανθρωποὶ νεοσσοὺς, σοῦ γίνονται ξενοδόχοι φιλότιμοι. Ἄτοπόν ἐστιν, ὦ Ἠλία, τοὺς μὲν κόρακας μεσίτας γίνεσθαι πρὸς σὲ τῆς παρ᾽ ἐμοῦ φιλανθρωπίας· σὲ δὲ μεσίτην τοῖς Ἰουδαίοις μὴ γίνεσθαι τῆς παρ᾽ ἐμοῦ κατ᾽ [II, 810] αὐτῶν τιμωρίας. Αἰδέσθητι τὴν τῶν κοράκων μεταβολὴν, καὶ γένου περὶ τοὺς Ἰουδαίους χρηστός. [Mē tosautē para soi meta Ioudaiōn misoteknia, hosē tois koraxi kata tōn neossōn tōn oikeiōn. all᾽ hora nyn metabeblēmenous tous korakas. hora tēn ekeinōn, ō Ēlia, philanthrōpian. hoi peri tous oikeious apanthrōpoi neossous, sou ginontai xenodochoi philotimoi. Atopon estin, ō Ēlia, tous men korakas mesitas ginesthai pros se tēs par᾽ emou philanthrōpias; se de mesitēn tois Ioudaiois mē ginesthai tēs par᾽ emou kat᾽ autōn timōrias. Aidesthēti tēn tōn korakōn metabolēn, kai genou peri tous Ioudaious chrēstos.] Do not hold the Jews, your children, in as great hatred as the ravens hold their chicks. Yet see the ravens now changed. See, O Elias, their kindness. They who are inhuman toward their own chicks show themselves generous hosts toward you. It is absurd, O Elias, that the ravens should be mediators of my kindness toward you, while you do not intercede for the Jews, whom I am punishing. Marvel at the change in the ravens, and be kind toward the Jews. There are some among more recent writers who hold that God the more justly exacted this service from the ravens, that they should feed his prophet, because of the greater care with which he feeds them when, still chicks, they are abandoned by their parents, as they prove from the words of Job, David, and Christ himself, which we have explained otherwise.

The brook Cerith, or Carith, at which this miracle took place, is thought to be the same as the brook Kana, or of the reed-bed, mentioned in Ios. XVI, 8. and XVII, 9. I would readily believe this, and that it was called קנה kana from the abundance of reeds in which Elias lay hidden. Like the one of whom the greatest of poets says,
